title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-Teacher Adaptive On-Policy Self-Distillation

paper.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-Teacher Adaptive On-Policy Self-Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to + 5.9 +5.9 over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ) has emerged as a promising paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), showing superiority over other post-training paradigms like Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (e.g., GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) ). In OPSD, the same model serves as both student and teacher. The student generates rollout responses, while the teacher provides supervision with access to privileged references, such as reference solutions. Compared with RLVR, OPSD provides dense token-level learning signals beyond sparse outcome rewards. Compared with SFT, it trains on trajectories sampled by the student itself, mitigating the exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) . Despite these advantages, recent studies ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ; Harne et al., 2026 ; Armandpour et al., 2026 ) reveal that OPSD can also suffer from degraded reasoning performance, which stems from the highly informative references exposed to the teacher. It may induce overly sharp teacher distributions, producing supervision that is poorly aligned with the student’s learning dynamics (e.g., suppressing uncertainty ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) ). A line of work ( Tan and Hong, 2026 ; Han et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026c ) has attempted to address this student-teacher mismatch through adaptive reference exposure. Rather than providing the teacher with the complete reference, it adjusts how much of the reference the teacher receives based on the student’s learning dynamics, such as the student-teacher gap. However, these methods adapt at the response level. Although reference exposure may vary across responses, it remains fixed across tokens within each response. In other words, all tokens in a rollout are supervised by the same teacher. In this paper, we challenge this consensus by arguing: The adaptive teacher should operate at the token level, because every token requires its own dedicated teacher. Figure 1: Token-level learning signals induced by different teachers for the same response. Teachers agree at some positions but provide opposing signals at others, motivating token-level teacher selection. Additional details on this visualization are provided in Appendix A . A teacher that provides useful guidance at one token may be less suitable at another, even within the same response. Rather than treating it with the same teacher, each token in the response merits consideration with its own preferred teacher. As illustrated in Figure 1 , when different teachers are applied to the same response, they can provide similar learning signals for some tokens but disagree on the direction of supervision for others. This suggests that not only each response, but also each token, may have distinct teacher preferences. While some prior work ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Hao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ; Ke et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026a ) has explored token selection for post-training (e.g., focusing solely on high-entropy tokens ( Wang et al., 2026c ) ), how to validate our claim is challenging, and how to adaptively identify the preferred teacher for each token remains unexplored. To answer these, we conduct a teacher-intervention pilot study ( Section 4 ) to quantify the token-level teacher preference. As shown in Figure 2 , we preserve a student-generated prefix, allow a candidate teacher to generate a short continuation at a selected token position, and then return control to the student to complete the response. The accuracy gain from this “student-teacher-student” relay over pure student generation serves as a proxy for the teacher preference at that token position. A large gain implies a compatible teacher for that position, while a small gain suggests the opposite. Interestingly, the results are simple, yet clear and compelling. First, teacher preferences differ across tokens, even within the same response. Second, at the token level, majority voting yields a subset of reliable teachers, and the preferred teacher always exhibits a large student-teacher KL distance. The first finding validates our claim, and the second finding motivates a practical rule for token-level teacher selection. Based on these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. As shown in Figure 3 , MTA-OPSD constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, by varying the truncation strategy and exposure ratio of the privileged reference. During training, rather than using a fixed teacher for all tokens in the same response, each token adaptively selects its own teacher from the multi-teacher pool based on its preference, through majority voting followed by KL-based selection. Our token-level adaptive OPSD design is simple yet effective, precisely addressing the student-teacher mismatch. By assigning each token its preferred teacher, MTA-OPSD provides a more balanced learning signal rather than an overly sharp, rigid teacher distribution from a single teacher. We evaluate MTA-OPSD on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and it consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to + 5.9 +5.9 over the base model. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We quantify the teacher preference across tokens via a teacher-intervention pilot study, validating that preferred teachers can differ from token to token within the same response. We further reveal that the token-level preferred teacher can be identified through majority voting and KL-based selection. • We propose MTA-OPSD, the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. By constructing a multi-teacher pool as the supervision source, our approach enables each token to adaptively select its preferred teacher under the guidance of majority voting and KL divergence, effectively addressing the student-teacher mismatch. • We conduct extensive experiments across various models on mathematical reasoning tasks, demonstrating that our approach achieves superior reasoning performance compared to existing OPSD methods. Furthermore, we empirically analyze comprehensive ablation studies, paving the way for future advances in this field.

sections.heading: 2.1 On-policy Distillation and On-Policy Self-distillation
sections.text: Knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a student model by training on the teacher’s soft output distributions. Early approaches ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ; Jiao et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) leveraged it to sequence-level distillation, establishing the dominant off-policy distillation approaches. ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) extended it to On-policy Distillation (OPD), addressing the exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) mismatch by shifting the training distribution to the student’s own generations. Despite the rapid progress of OPD, the paradigm relies on a separate, typically stronger teacher model, which may be unavailable or expensive to maintain. To address this challenge, OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) removes this requirement by instantiating the teacher and student from the same model. Under this setting, the teacher and student share the same model, but the teacher is granted access to a privileged reference unavailable to the student. However, recent studies ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Kaur et al., 2026 ; Harne et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) reveal a persistent mismatch in OPSD. In particular, a highly informative reference can induce an overly sharp teacher distribution and create a mismatch between the teacher’s supervision and the student’s learning dynamics. These observations motivate the line of research for adaptive OPSD methods.

sections.heading: 2.2 Adaptive On-Policy Self-distillation
sections.text: Adaptive OPSD seeks to align the teacher supervision with the student’s learning dynamics. Rather than exposing the complete privileged reference, existing methods ( Tan and Hong, 2026 ; Han et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026c ) control its content or exposure ratio using mechanisms such as learned reference-exposure schedules. By varying the amount of privileged references available to the teacher, these methods aim to avoid overly sharp supervision while retaining the benefits of dense learning signals. However, these methods adapt at the response level, where all tokens in the response share the same teacher and the same privileged reference. In contrast, we identify that each token needs its own teacher as tokens have distinct teacher preferences ( Section 4 ), and further propose our token-level multi-teacher adaptive OPSD method.

sections.text: OPSD is a special case of OPD. sections.heading: 5 Method
sections.text: Based on the findings in Section 4.2 , we propose Multi-Teacher Adaptive OPSD (MTA-OPSD), a simple yet effective framework for token-level adaptive OPSD. As illustrated in Figure 3 , rather than using a single teacher, MTA-OPSD constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers conditioned on different variants of the privileged reference. Through majority voting followed by KL-based selection, it assigns each token its preferred teacher. This ensures that different tokens within the same response receive supervision from their respective teachers.

They differ from each other only in the privileged references on which they are conditioned: R = { r 1 , r 2 , ⋯ , r K } , R=\{r_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{K}\}, (8) which leads to the next-token distribution of each teacher as: p T k = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , r k ) . p_{T_{k}}=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,r_{k}). (9) Each r k r_{k} differs from each other by its truncation way and exposure ratio of the full reference. An example of our multi-teacher pool is provided in Appendix F . sections.heading: 5.4 Discussion
sections.text: The mechanism of our method can be understood as decoupling the reliability of the supervision direction from the informativeness of the supervision signal. Majority voting first determines whether the teacher pool collectively supports or opposes the student-generated token y i y^{i} , KL-based selection then identifies the most informative teacher aligned with that direction. This ordering is crucial: KL distance is not used as a standalone measure of teacher quality, but only after directional consensus has filtered out potentially unreliable teachers. Specifically, when V M ​ ( c i ) = 1 V_{M}(c_{i})=1 , the majority teachers in M maj ​ ( c i ) M_{\mathrm{maj}}(c_{i}) assign a higher probability to y i y^{i} than the student itself, and selecting the teacher with the largest KL therefore reinforces the student’s current choice. Meanwhile, the selected teacher can also provide a substantially different overall probability distribution. Consequently, the supervision can strengthen the sampled token without being limited to simply imitating it, thereby retaining informative probabilities for other plausible predictions and potentially reducing overfitting to the student’s current trajectory. When V M ​ ( c i ) = − 1 V_{M}(c_{i})=-1 , the majority teachers assign a lower probability to y i y^{i} , and the sampled token is collectively regarded as a less preferred choice. In this case, a teacher with a small KL distance may only weakly downweight this token or remain too close to the student distribution. In contrast, the farthest teacher is more likely to redistribute probability mass toward different candidate tokens, providing a stronger corrective signal together with more distinct alternative prediction directions. Such supervision may therefore help the student move away from a potentially erroneous local choice rather than merely making a marginal adjustment to it.

sections.heading: 6.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: Additional experiment setup details are provided in Appendix C . Models and Datasets. We evaluate models from the Qwen3 family ( Yang et al., 2025 ) at three scales: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B, all with thinking mode enabled during both training and validation. We conduct experiments across mathematical reasoning tasks. The training data is drawn from DeepMath-103K ( He et al., 2026 ) , and we evaluate on AMC23 ( MAA, 2023 ) , AIME24 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2024 ) , and AIME25 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2025 ) . Baselines. We compare our method against two fixed-teacher OPSD methods and one adaptive OPSD method: (1) OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , which performs dense-logit distillation using forward KL with token-wise pointwise KL clipping; (2) SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , which performs dense-logit distillation using Jensen–Shannon divergence; and (3) Paint ( Tan and Hong, 2026 ) , which adaptively determines the reference-exposure ratio according to the student-teacher gap. Implementation Details. All baselines and our method use dataset-provided ground-truth reference solutions as the privileged information, and all contexts include both the reasoning trace and the final answer. We use identical training and evaluation settings across all methods, with maximum generation lengths of 4096 tokens during training and 38912 tokens during validation. The multi-teacher pool contains seven teacher configurations: {full reference, prefix- 0.5 0.5 , prefix- 0.75 0.75 , suffix- 0.5 0.5 , suffix- 0.75 0.75 , random-span- 0.5 0.5 , random-span- 0.75 0.75 } 4 4 4 The truncation strategy determines which part of the reference is retained. For example, prefix truncation with an exposure ratio of 0.5 0.5 retains the first half of the reference. The final answer is retained under every truncation setting to ensure a fair comparison. . We train each method for 300 steps, evaluate checkpoints every 50 steps on the test set, and report its best Avg@12 results.

We first investigate whether the multi-teacher pool provides more effective supervision than any individual teacher. In Table 8 , we compare our method with training using each teacher configuration from the pool independently. Although the effectiveness of individual teachers varies from each other, MTA-OPSD achieves the highest score on both average and individual benchmarks. These results suggest that the multi-teacher pool offers diverse, sufficient, and complementary learning signals. Effect of Token-Level Teacher Assignment. The multi-teacher pool is accompanied by the token-level adaptive teacher assignment. The previous ablation establishes the value of the former, but does not isolate the contribution of the latter. We therefore retain the same multi-teacher pool and compare MTA-OPSD with two alternative assignment strategies: (1) Random teacher selection from the pool for each token, and (2) averaging the distillation losses from all teachers. As shown in Table 8 , MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms both alternatives on every benchmark. These show that the gains do not arise solely from multiple teachers; selecting a suitable teacher for each token is critical to using the teacher pool effectively. Teacher-Assignment Dynamics. We also investigate how frequently each teacher is selected throughout training. The assignments are distributed relatively evenly across the teacher pool, indicating that the selection mechanism does not collapse to a single dominant teacher. We also observe that, under the same truncation strategy, a higher reference-exposure ratio does not necessarily produce a larger student-teacher KL distance, as discussed in Appendix E . This observation further suggests that existing adaptive methods of adjusting reference exposure alone cannot determine teacher suitability. Effect of Majority Voting and KL-Based Selection. MTA-OPSD selects a teacher in two steps: majority voting and KL-based selection. Table 8 presents the contribution of each step, where the second row is our default setting. MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms all variants, further validating the effectiveness of our design: majority voting first identifies a reliable teacher subset, and KL-based selection chooses a teacher from that subset.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We present MTA-OPSD, the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. A teacher-intervention study shows that teacher preferences vary across tokens and motivates our two-step token-level adaptive teacher selection strategy: majority voting with KL-based selection. Future work may explore self-evolving teacher pools and more stable multi-teacher training.

In this case, we break the tie according to the magnitudes of the corresponding advantage signals. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to + 5.9 +5.9 over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD . † † footnotetext: Correspondence to: Yifu Luo ( yifu599@gmail.com ) and Chuang Ma ( ma.chuang.52h@st.kyoto-u.ac.jp ). 1 Introduction On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ) has emerged as a promising paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), showing superiority over other post-training paradigms like Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (e.g., GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) ). In OPSD, the same model serves as both student and teacher. The student generates rollout responses, while the teacher provides supervision with access to privileged references, such as reference solutions. Compared with RLVR, OPSD provides dense token-level learning signals beyond sparse outcome rewards. Compared with SFT, it trains on trajectories sampled by the student itself, mitigating the exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) . Despite these advantages, recent studies ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ; Harne et al., 2026 ; Armandpour et al., 2026 ) reveal that OPSD can also suffer from degraded reasoning performance, which stems from the highly informative references exposed to the teacher. It may induce overly sharp teacher distributions, producing supervision that is poorly aligned with the student’s learning dynamics (e.g., suppressing uncertainty ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) ). A line of work ( Tan and Hong, 2026 ; Han et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026c ) has attempted to address this student-teacher mismatch through adaptive reference exposure. Rather than providing the teacher with the complete reference, it adjusts how much of the reference the teacher receives based on the student’s learning dynamics, such as the student-teacher gap. However, these methods adapt at the response level. Although reference exposure may vary across responses, it remains fixed across tokens within each response. In other words, all tokens in a rollout are supervised by the same teacher. In this paper, we challenge this consensus by arguing: The adaptive teacher should operate at the token level, because every token requires its own dedicated teacher. Figure 1: Token-level learning signals induced by different teachers for the same response. Teachers agree at some positions but provide opposing signals at others, motivating token-level teacher selection. Additional details on this visualization are provided in Appendix A . A teacher that provides useful guidance at one token may be less suitable at another, even within the same response. Rather than treating it with the same teacher, each token in the response merits consideration with its own preferred teacher. As illustrated in Figure 1 , when different teachers are applied to the same response, they can provide similar learning signals for some tokens but disagree on the direction of supervision for others. This suggests that not only each response, but also each token, may have distinct teacher preferences. While some prior work ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Hao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ; Ke et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026a ) has explored token selection for post-training (e.g., focusing solely on high-entropy tokens ( Wang et al., 2026c ) ), how to validate our claim is challenging, and how to adaptively identify the preferred teacher for each token remains unexplored. To answer these, we conduct a teacher-intervention pilot study ( Section 4 ) to quantify the token-level teacher preference. As shown in Figure 2 , we preserve a student-generated prefix, allow a candidate teacher to generate a short continuation at a selected token position, and then return control to the student to complete the response. The accuracy gain from this “student-teacher-student” relay over pure student generation serves as a proxy for the teacher preference at that token position. A large gain implies a compatible teacher for that position, while a small gain suggests the opposite. Interestingly, the results are simple, yet clear and compelling. First, teacher preferences differ across tokens, even within the same response. Second, at the token level, majority voting yields a subset of reliable teachers, and the preferred teacher always exhibits a large student-teacher KL distance. The first finding validates our claim, and the second finding motivates a practical rule for token-level teacher selection. Based on these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. As shown in Figure 3 , MTA-OPSD constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, by varying the truncation strategy and exposure ratio of the privileged reference. During training, rather than using a fixed teacher for all tokens in the same response, each token adaptively selects its own teacher from the multi-teacher pool based on its preference, through majority voting followed by KL-based selection. Our token-level adaptive OPSD design is simple yet effective, precisely addressing the student-teacher mismatch. By assigning each token its preferred teacher, MTA-OPSD provides a more balanced learning signal rather than an overly sharp, rigid teacher distribution from a single teacher. We evaluate MTA-OPSD on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and it consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to + 5.9 +5.9 over the base model. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We quantify the teacher preference across tokens via a teacher-intervention pilot study, validating that preferred teachers can differ from token to token within the same response. We further reveal that the token-level preferred teacher can be identified through majority voting and KL-based selection. • We propose MTA-OPSD, the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. By constructing a multi-teacher pool as the supervision source, our approach enables each token to adaptively select its preferred teacher under the guidance of majority voting and KL divergence, effectively addressing the student-teacher mismatch. • We conduct extensive experiments across various models on mathematical reasoning tasks, demonstrating that our approach achieves superior reasoning performance compared to existing OPSD methods. Furthermore, we empirically analyze comprehensive ablation studies, paving the way for future advances in this field. 2 Related Work 2.1 On-policy Distillation and On-Policy Self-distillation Knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a student model by training on the teacher’s soft output distributions. Early approaches ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ; Jiao et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) leveraged it to sequence-level distillation, establishing the dominant off-policy distillation approaches. ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) extended it to On-policy Distillation (OPD), addressing the exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) mismatch by shifting the training distribution to the student’s own generations. Despite the rapid progress of OPD, the paradigm relies on a separate, typically stronger teacher model, which may be unavailable or expensive to maintain. To address this challenge, OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) removes this requirement by instantiating the teacher and student from the same model. Under this setting, the teacher and student share the same model, but the teacher is granted access to a privileged reference unavailable to the student. However, recent studies ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Kaur et al., 2026 ; Harne et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) reveal a persistent mismatch in OPSD. In particular, a highly informative reference can induce an overly sharp teacher distribution and create a mismatch between the teacher’s supervision and the student’s learning dynamics. These observations motivate the line of research for adaptive OPSD methods. 2.2 Adaptive On-Policy Self-distillation Adaptive OPSD seeks to align the teacher supervision with the student’s learning dynamics. Rather than exposing the complete privileged reference, existing methods ( Tan and Hong, 2026 ; Han et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026c ) control its content or exposure ratio using mechanisms such as learned reference-exposure schedules. By varying the amount of privileged references available to the teacher, these methods aim to avoid overly sharp supervision while retaining the benefits of dense learning signals. However, these methods adapt at the response level, where all tokens in the response share the same teacher and the same privileged reference. In contrast, we identify that each token needs its own teacher as tokens have distinct teacher preferences ( Section 4 ), and further propose our token-level multi-teacher adaptive OPSD method. 3 Preliminaries OPSD is a special case of OPD. Majority voting first determines whether the teacher pool collectively supports or opposes the student-generated token y i y^{i} , KL-based selection then identifies the most informative teacher aligned with that direction. This ordering is crucial: KL distance is not used as a standalone measure of teacher quality, but only after directional consensus has filtered out potentially unreliable teachers. Specifically, when V M ​ ( c i ) = 1 V_{M}(c_{i})=1 , the majority teachers in M maj ​ ( c i ) M_{\mathrm{maj}}(c_{i}) assign a higher probability to y i y^{i} than the student itself, and selecting the teacher with the largest KL therefore reinforces the student’s current choice. Meanwhile, the selected teacher can also provide a substantially different overall probability distribution. Consequently, the supervision can strengthen the sampled token without being limited to simply imitating it, thereby retaining informative probabilities for other plausible predictions and potentially reducing overfitting to the student’s current trajectory. When V M ​ ( c i ) = − 1 V_{M}(c_{i})=-1 , the majority teachers assign a lower probability to y i y^{i} , and the sampled token is collectively regarded as a less preferred choice. In this case, a teacher with a small KL distance may only weakly downweight this token or remain too close to the student distribution. In contrast, the farthest teacher is more likely to redistribute probability mass toward different candidate tokens, providing a stronger corrective signal together with more distinct alternative prediction directions. Such supervision may therefore help the student move away from a potentially erroneous local choice rather than merely making a marginal adjustment to it. 6 Experiments 6.1 Experiment Setup Additional experiment setup details are provided in Appendix C . We first investigate whether the multi-teacher pool provides more effective supervision than any individual teacher. In Table 8 , we compare our method with training using each teacher configuration from the pool independently. Although the effectiveness of individual teachers varies from each other, MTA-OPSD achieves the highest score on both average and individual benchmarks. These results suggest that the multi-teacher pool offers diverse, sufficient, and complementary learning signals. Effect of Token-Level Teacher Assignment. The multi-teacher pool is accompanied by the token-level adaptive teacher assignment. The previous ablation establishes the value of the former, but does not isolate the contribution of the latter. We therefore retain the same multi-teacher pool and compare MTA-OPSD with two alternative assignment strategies: (1) Random teacher selection from the pool for each token, and (2) averaging the distillation losses from all teachers. As shown in Table 8 , MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms both alternatives on every benchmark. These show that the gains do not arise solely from multiple teachers; selecting a suitable teacher for each token is critical to using the teacher pool effectively. Teacher-Assignment Dynamics. We also investigate how frequently each teacher is selected throughout training. The assignments are distributed relatively evenly across the teacher pool, indicating that the selection mechanism does not collapse to a single dominant teacher. We also observe that, under the same truncation strategy, a higher reference-exposure ratio does not necessarily produce a larger student-teacher KL distance, as discussed in Appendix E . This observation further suggests that existing adaptive methods of adjusting reference exposure alone cannot determine teacher suitability. Effect of Majority Voting and KL-Based Selection. MTA-OPSD selects a teacher in two steps: majority voting and KL-based selection. Table 8 presents the contribution of each step, where the second row is our default setting. MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms all variants, further validating the effectiveness of our design: majority voting first identifies a reliable teacher subset, and KL-based selection chooses a teacher from that subset. 7 Conclusion We present MTA-OPSD, the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. A teacher-intervention study shows that teacher preferences vary across tokens and motivates our two-step token-level adaptive teacher selection strategy: majority voting with KL-based selection. Future work may explore self-evolving teacher pools and more stable multi-teacher training.
